claims.text: Conventionally sintered single-phase ZrB2 requires processing temperatures above 2300 °C.
Lower-temperature-processed ZrB2 is vulnerable to oxidation and liquid plating-metal corrosion.
The proposed material has equimolar Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta, and Ti on the metal sublattice of a diboride.
The equimolar Zr-Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti formulation will form a high-entropy diboride solid solution during sintering at or below 1700 °C.
High-temperature structural applications require a combination of strength, oxidation resistance, and corrosion resistance.
The intervention will produce a homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy diboride.
Lattice distortion and grain-boundary engineering in the high-entropy diboride will promote more effective sintering.
The high-entropy microstructure will enable in situ formation of a protective, coherent oxide layer.
Increased configurational entropy will stabilize the diboride phase at lower processing temperatures.
The multicomponent formulation will enhance diffusion during sintering.
The multicomponent formulation will suppress undesirable phase segregation.
Complex multicomponent chemistry will facilitate formation of a protective surface oxide during service.
A uniform microstructure will reduce rapid-corrosion sites and thereby improve liquid-metal corrosion resistance.
The proposed high-entropy diboride will achieve full densification at a sintering temperature of 1700 °C or less.
The proposed material will have mechanical strength comparable to or greater than traditionally processed single-phase ZrB2.
The proposed material will have significantly better oxidation resistance than single-phase ZrB2 and earlier lower-temperature specimens.
The proposed material will have better corrosion durability in liquid plating environments than single-phase ZrB2 and earlier lower-temperature specimens.
The anticipated performance boundary includes sintering at or below 1700 °C and service at temperatures typical of high-temperature structural components.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome permits mechanical strength merely comparable to conventional ZrB2, but the falsification rule requires the mechanical properties to statistically and significantly exceed those of the comparator.

The design specifies only conventionally sintered pure ZrB2 above 2300 °C as the control, whereas the falsification rule compares the high-entropy material with low-temperature-processed pure ZrB2, a control not included in the stated design.
